slides.0.title: Mendoza I: overview, Luján de Cuyo and Maipú
slides.0.subtitle: Mendoza's tiers of geographical indication and its traditional heartland
slides.1.title: Mendoza: the heart of Argentina
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Dominance
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Mendoza accounts for over half of national output and 84.4% of Malbec (Level 1)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Three traditional zones
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Geographical indications run down to the department level — Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and the Uco Valley — and then to smaller districts
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Irrigation and rain
slides.1.highlights.2.content: A semi-arid continental climate with under 250 mm of rain a year, reliant on snowmelt from the Mendoza, Tunuyán and other rivers
slides.1.content: Understand Mendoza's department tiers first, and the origin names on labels make sense.
slides.2.title: Luján de Cuyo
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Altitude and area
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Vineyards at about 800–1,100 m over some 15,000 ha (Wine With Seth); alluvial fans built by the Mendoza River and Andean tributaries give rocky, sandy, free-draining soils
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Five well-known districts
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Agrelo (about 950–1,050 m), Las Compuertas (about 1,050–1,100 m, the highest), Vistalba (about 950–1,000 m), Perdriel and Ugarteche
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Malbec style
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Decanter (2019): Las Compuertas Malbec is firm and suited to long cellaring; Vistalba is gentler and can be drunk younger; Agrelo (about 9,000 ha) is deep in colour with black fruit and soft, sweet tannins
slides.2.content: Luján de Cuyo is Malbec's traditional heartland, with style shifting by altitude and location within it.
slides.3.title: The Luján de Cuyo DOC and Maipú
slides.3.highlights.0.title: DOC rules (single source)
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Wine With Seth: at least 85% Malbec, vineyards at least 10 years old and more than 5,000 vines per hectare; a 2021 relaunch allowed drip irrigation and a 15% blending allowance. Only about 519 ha are DOC-certified, so it is a choice of a few producers; the start date differs across sources
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Maipú
slides.3.highlights.1.content: South of Mendoza city, with vineyards at about 640–1,000 m, warmer than the Uco Valley; European varieties were planted from the mid-19th century and Trapiche was founded in 1883
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Districts of Maipú
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Barrancas (warmer, more clay, riper fruit), Lunlunta (tighter structure, finer tannins, often a premium source) and Coquimbito (transitional to Luján de Cuyo)
slides.3.content: Maipú is warmer than Luján de Cuyo, and its wines are usually fuller and a little higher in alcohol.
